CARGO THEFT

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Trucks are looted every single day in South Africa – we expose this growing trend and ask what it costs the economy?

Unique Selling Point:
SHOCKING FOOTAGE & A COOL STING

Summary:
90% of what you buy and consume is transported by road – that’s over R456 billion worth of goods on the road every year – making the transport industry a prime target for opportunistic and organised thieves.

We expose this crime trend – looking at the contributing factors and impacts on the economy.

Further information:
When a truck breaks down in certain rural areas – you can be sure that the cargo will be gone in a matter of minutes. In some cases where roads are challenging and trucks moved at reduced speeds – thieves simply get on and loot the moving truck.

WHO’S BEHIND IT?
It’s both opportunistic and organized. People from surrounding communities will loot when the opportunity arises. While others will specifically target trucks and come prepared with vehicles to move the goods.

WHY DOESN’T ANYONE SPEAK OUT?
Firstly – stolen goods are FREE – so if you are to sell it even at a reduced price you are still making a profit. Should you buy it at a reduced price – you are still winning because it’s cheaper than market value. So no one wants to snitch on the looting thieves – because everyone except the transporter benefits.

IMPACT ON TRANSPORT INDUSTRY
The economy looses millions of rands annually to stolen cargo. It cost the transporters increased insurance premiums and pushes up transport costs which eventually translates to increased consumer goods prices.

SECONDARY DAMAGE
But it goes beyond the loss of the cargo. Often trucks are damaged – tyres slashed, tarps cut – this all costs money and means that the trucks will not be operational for a few days costing even more money in lost revenue.

VIOLENCE
In many instances the looters have turned violent when transporters and the police have tried to stop them. Some drivers are fearful of driving certain routes with consumer goods. There are cases of drivers being shot at, attacked with broken bottles.

There have even been horrific cases where drivers have died in accidents and looters continued stealing the cargo despite the driver’s body lying there.

POLICE
The police is not effective at all. There are videos where they simply stand by as the looters carry away cargo without intervening.

SECURITY
This type of cargo theft has opened up a market for armed security escorts. 95% of big transport companies make used of additional security to escort their trucks through certain areas. If they don’t they will get targeted.

HOW TO DO IT
- FOOTAGE – we have great videos of cargo being stolen from moving trucks and accident scenes.
- STING – we have a transporter that has offered us a load to move through an area where we expect stealing to take place. We will wait nearby and intervene – filming everything as it happens.

INTERVIEWS
- BIG TRANSPORTER – impact from a national perspective, the extent of the looting and threats to drivers.
- SMALL TRANSPORTER – often they can’t afford the security and are at a greater risk.
- ARMED ESCORTS – they explain the MO and level opportunism vs organized efforts.
- POLICE – why aren’t they acting – it’s criminality right in front of them.
- INSURANCE – impact on the economy – extent of the losses.
- DRIVERS – We hear first hand from drivers that have been attacked and threatened and why they are scared to drive certain routes.


Extra Budget Items:
I'll need an extra half day with Devi - we are filming between Port Shepstone and Kokstad and then in Durban - the travel time from the airport to the sting location is roughly 2 and half hours each way. So we'll loose 5 hours of shoot time in travel time.

Press Release:


Cargo Theft
The N2 between KZN and the Eastern Cape has become a treacherous route. Violent looters target
moving trucks, ripping cargo off the back of the trailer and within minutes, making off with millions of Rands
worth of goods. It’s costing the economy billions, so why has nothing been done to stop the looting? Carte
Blanche exposes this growing trend.

Script:


SCRIPT

VO: It looks like a free for all…. People taking all they can carry in a matter of minutes. But it’s not free – it’s actually theft.

LINK: It might look like petty crime, a bag of sugar, a sheep, a crate of beer – but when you add up the loads across the country it’s a massive hit to the economy.

GLYNN: these loads are probably going for anything from R350k up – it’s not just small losses when an entire load is stolen.

VO: Cargo Theft is rife. There is at least one incident like this across South Africa every day says Transport Insurance Assessor Glynn Millard.

GLYNN: // almost everyone in South Africa seems to think they are entitled to cargo once it’s fallen off a vehicle. // not just the poor community, but also the drivers of passing vehicles, trucks, they all stop and load their vehicles.

VO: In this video, people are raiding a beer truck – watch as this man stops his combi and then joins in.

While food and booze are high-risk loads to transport - everything is up for the taking – even cash-in-transit trucks.

GLYNN: We’ve had all sorts stolen – from bags of fertiliser to gas bottles – you name it, it will get stolen.

JANI: We’ve had a 30 ton load in half hour that there’s not a piece of chicken of left, a sheep truck with real live sheep – gone!

VO: Jani van Jaarsveld runs a recovery towing company in KZN – she says when they go out to recover broken down or accident damaged trucks – it’s like the wild west.

JANI: It’s unreal, you cannot explain it to someone – you cannot get control of the situation.

VO: KZN Police Spokesperson, Brigadier Jay Naicker acknowledges even the police battle to control crowds at these scenes.

JAY: It’s even more shocking when there is accident and people are dying and the truck is being looted because of it’s load. People may need serious attention and the police then have to concentrate their efforts on preventing the people from looting the truck.

VO: But stationary trucks are not the only targets.

In this video you can a see man on the back of a truck, there is another man inside passing him items that he drops one by one.

This is not unusual says small operator Neil Chetty.

NEIL: Our robberies are more when vehicles are moving up hill – and moving slowly. Generally the guys cut our tarps, break the locks on the doors.

VO: He does trips to the Eastern Cape – his trucks have been knocked 5 times this year alone.

NEIL: IN my case, transport furniture
DEVI: take entire two lounge suites
NEIL: They would just open and pull off one or two pieces of the lounge set and throw it on the side of the road.

VO: The N2 route from Port Shepstone on the KZN South Coast through to the Eastern Cape has become notorious for cargo theft and looting.

Sewraj Girdhurparsadh provides armed escorts for trucks. His company alone does roughly 12 000 trips every month.

SEW: Your N2 running through the EC is very much different from your N1 / N3 in this sense that it runs plonk through the middle of townships and the terrain makes for very hilly and windy uphill and downhills where trucks can not run through at decent speed.

LINK: Cargo theft is not about looters just taking a chance – in some cases it’s quite organised with spotters along the freeway.

SPOTTER: The job of the spotter it is to see the trucks, that trucks is going up the hill is being escorted or not, it’s not being escorted

VO: This man is a spotter, lets call him Vusi, he lives along the N2 on the KZN South Coast.

SPOTTER: – if it’s not being escorted, we go to the trucks and jump to the trucks while it is moving up in the mountain

SEW: This is what they do – 24 hours a day – they are watching high – in effect
they see the truck more than the truck owners.

VO: Vusi realised the earning potential and perfected his spotting skills – knowing what’s inside the truck would help him choose better targets.

SPOTTER: I became the master now, knowing the truck that is coming down – when I see the truck I will know this truck is carrying the sugar, this one is carrying the alcohol, this one is carrying the mixed veggies.

VO: Guys like Vusi operate in groups of 3 or 4 – this is a profession for them, says Sewraj.

SEW: The criminal or community’s mind set is it’s insured – why worry?

VO: But this perception that cargo is fair game because it’s covered by insurance is a misnomer – somebody always pays.

GLYNN: // The costs are being absorbed by the consumer – the everyday South African is suffering these losses because the prices are going up to cover for all these types of losses.

LINK: Getting to the loot – means trucks are damaged – tarps are cut, tyres are slashed, adding to the losses.

TED: It’s all peripheral damage, but it all adds up at the end of day to more costs to us as transporters. // It does has quite a significant impact on the bottom line but we don’t have a choice

VO: Transporters like Ted Hughes are having to upgrade their trucks and are taking preventative measures like installing spikes and mesh in an effort to deter thieves.

TED: The mesh is incorporated in the tarpaulin here, as you can see here – just this square mesh – so they can get a knife through there but once they come here they can’t.

VO: But it seems that cargo theft is linked to the economic situation in the country.

SPOTTER: I’m not scared of the police because at the end of the day what I am thinking is I have to put the food on the table there by the house I don’t put the police on my mind

VO: And with limited resources the police say – they can’t be everywhere all the time.

JAY: We deploy according to our crime threats and our crime patterns. Its vast stretches of road and we don’t have the resources to place permanently on the roads.

VO: Leaving the roads open to cargo thieves.

We wanted to see just how quickly cargo can disappear along the N2.

STING LINK: We’ve set up a decoy and the easiest product to get hold of – beer – it goes in the truck – let see who comes for it.

VO: We loaded some crates of empties to make the truck look full and off we went.

Our truck pulled over in an area known for looting. We put the hazards on and faked a breakdown.

Within minutes, this man with the pink beanie coming to inspect the load. Watch as he passes by slowly, peaking inside. He walks away, and then comes back, making a call while seemingly guarding the truck.

When his friends arrived they jumped in and made off with three crates of beer. Realising the coast was clear – they returned with more people who joined in.

STING LINK: So you’ve got people running away clearly behind me – // what is easy to tell – the people watching us right now – knew this was happening – they could see this was happening right from the very beginning. Let’s see what’s left of the load… ok we’ve got some wasted beer that’s fallen off the side.
STING LINK: Most of its gone, all we’re left with are the empties.

VO: While our decoy truck was looted peacefully – it’s not always the case says Jani.

JANI: We sometimes don’t even get a chance to recover the truck, - the people come from every where and they are dangerous – they’ve taken possession of the load because the load has now fallen in their area and this load belongs to them – you are not allowed to take anything from that accident scene.

VO: We spoke to two of Jani’s drivers - they asked not be identified.

DRIVER 1: When we get to the scene to get the vehicle they normally don’t want us to take away the vehicle because they are busy off loading – at most of the scenes they throw objects at us just to get us away from the scene.

DRIVER 2: There’s nothing I can actually do. They always get violent. When you come next to them, they want to kill you
DEVI: How do they threaten you?
DRIVER 2: They come with everything you can think of – they come with guns.

VO: These situations can get out of hand very quickly, with serious consequences.

DRIVER 1: someone ran across the road and threw a rock – I saw it when it was right next to the windscreen. I couldn’t duck it or anything – so all I could do is lift up my hand and cover my face.
DEVI: And the damage?
DRIVER 1: I had maxi facial and I got three metal plates on the right side of my face.

VO: These cargo thieves mean business.

SEW: You have your more organised guys that drops off guys that, offload the trucks and then come fetch the stuff as in a bakkie or a taxi

VO: Something the recovery drivers have witnessed.

DRIVER 2: There was a super link loaded with plank, there was security guards there everything – so when I pick the truck up – I got it on it’s wheels – the plank – the load fell – the guys that were guarding the load they were pointed with firearms – they want to help themselves to the load – tractors were there, vans were there
DEVI: Tractors?
DRIVER 2: Tractors! With trailers… they load everything.

VO: And with cargo theft not being a priority crime, very few arrests are made.

NEIL: There’s times when we opened up cases for stuff stolen but we never really got any feedback from there… I don’t know if the cases are getting investigated.

VO: Brigadier Naicker accepts there are challenges with these types of cases.

JAY: The investigation becomes a problem because the communities that benefit from it don’t talk. It’s very difficult.

SEW: It comes free to the criminal, he can sell it as reduced, almost for nothing and he’s still makes money. Needless to say the end- user is saving // they score as well // purely on the basis of this being a win – win – this aint going away.

VO: Spotter Vusi agrees, there’s even a black market for the stolen cargo.

SPOTTER: It’s easier to sell it to spaza shop. Lets say for example the 10kg rice is R100 by the store – now we are going to sell it for R50 – just to get the quick bucks.
DEVI: how much would you make from load?
SPOTTER: usually every week we were making about 6 grand, 6000 or 7000 each week because we were selling the things cheaper

VO: Vusi says there is a big demand for stolen goods.

SPOTTER: people from the spaza shops were starting to put the order to us - if they want the rice, if they want the sugar they came to us they put the orders – so, we take from the trucks.

JAY: And somehow people have the impression that if a truck is involved in an accident they are entitled to the load and that is not the case – there is an owner for those goods, and you can’t just remove it with out permission – it’s still theft.


 
PROMOS

PROMO1
VO: Cargo theft is rife in South Africa.

SEW: // The criminal or community’s mindset is it’s insured – why worry?

VO: If you add up the losses - it’s a massive hit to the economy.


PROMO 2
VO: Cargo theft is a growing trend in South Africa– everything is up for the taking - with entire loads disappearing in minutes.

GLYNN: We’ve had all sorts stolen – from bags of fertiliser to gas bottles – you name it, it will get stolen. // INT6 M3

PROMO 3

VO: Cargo Theft is more organised than you’d think – brazen gangs target specific trucks to get to the loot.

SPOTTER: we go to the trucks and jump to the trucks while it is moving up in the mountain // INT1 M2

VO: We expose this growing trend.

SEW: Your N2 running through the EC is very much different from your N1 / N3 in this sense that it runs plonk through the middle of townships and the terrain makes for very hilly and windy uphill and downhills where trucks can not run through at decent speed. LINK: Cargo theft is not about looters just taking a chance – in some cases it’s quite organised with spotters along the freeway. SPOTTER: The job of the spotter it is to see the trucks, that trucks is going up the hill is being escorted or not, it’s not being escorted VO: This man is a spotter, lets call him Vusi, he lives along the N2 on the KZN South Coast. SPOTTER: – if it’s not being escorted, we go to the trucks and jump to the trucks while it is moving up in the mountain SEW: This is what they do – 24 hours a day – they are watching high – in effect they see the truck more than the truck owners. VO: Vusi realised the earning potential and perfected his spotting skills – knowing what’s inside the truck would help him choose better targets. SPOTTER: I became the master now, knowing the truck that is coming down – when I see the truck I will know this truck is carrying the sugar, this one is carrying the alcohol, this one is carrying the mixed veggies. VO: Guys like Vusi operate in groups of 3 or 4 – this is a profession for them, says Sewraj. SEW: The criminal or community’s mind set is it’s insured – why worry? VO: But this perception that cargo is fair game because it’s covered by insurance is a misnomer – somebody always pays. GLYNN: // The costs are being absorbed by the consumer – the everyday South African is suffering these losses because the prices are going up to cover for all these types of losses. LINK: Getting to the loot – means trucks are damaged – tarps are cut, tyres are slashed, adding to the losses. TED: It’s all peripheral damage, but it all adds up at the end of day to more costs to us as transporters. // It does has quite a significant impact on the bottom line but we don’t have a choice VO: Transporters like Ted Hughes are having to upgrade their trucks and are taking preventative measures like installing spikes and mesh in an effort to deter thieves. TED: The mesh is incorporated in the tarpaulin here, as you can see here – just this square mesh – so they can get a knife through there but once they come here they can’t. VO: But it seems that cargo theft is linked to the economic situation in the country. SPOTTER: I’m not scared of the police because at the end of the day what I am thinking is I have to put the food on the table there by the house I don’t put the police on my mind VO: And with limited resources the police say – they can’t be everywhere all the time. JAY: We deploy according to our crime threats and our crime patterns. Its vast stretches of road and we don’t have the resources to place permanently on the roads. VO: Leaving the roads open to cargo thieves. We wanted to see just how quickly cargo can disappear along the N2. STING LINK: We’ve set up a decoy and the easiest product to get hold of – beer – it goes in the truck – let see who comes for it. VO: We loaded some crates of empties to make the truck look full and off we went. Our truck pulled over in an area known for looting. We put the hazards on and faked a breakdown. Within minutes, this man with the pink beanie coming to inspect the load. Watch as he passes by slowly, peaking inside. He walks away, and then comes back, making a call while seemingly guarding the truck. When his friends arrived they jumped in and made off with three crates of beer. Realising the coast was clear – they returned with more people who joined in. STING LINK: So you’ve got people running away clearly behind me – // what is easy to tell – the people watching us right now – knew this was happening – they could see this was happening right from the very beginning. Let’s see what’s left of the load… ok we’ve got some wasted beer that’s fallen off the side. STING LINK: Most of its gone, all we’re left with are the empties. VO: While our decoy truck was looted peacefully – it’s not always the case says Jani. JANI: We sometimes don’t even get a chance to recover the truck, - the people come from every where and they are dangerous – they’ve taken possession of the load because the load has now fallen in their area and this load belongs to them – you are not allowed to take anything from that accident scene. VO: We spoke to two of Jani’s drivers - they asked not be identified. DRIVER 1: When we get to the scene to get the vehicle they normally don’t want us to take away the vehicle because they are busy off loading – at most of the scenes they throw objects at us just to get us away from the scene. DRIVER 2: There’s nothing I can actually do. They always get violent. When you come next to them, they want to kill you DEVI: How do they threaten you? DRIVER 2: They come with everything you can think of – they come with guns. VO: These situations can get out of hand very quickly, with serious consequences. DRIVER 1: someone ran across the road and threw a rock – I saw it when it was right next to the windscreen. I couldn’t duck it or anything – so all I could do is lift up my hand and cover my face. DEVI: And the damage? DRIVER 1: I had maxi facial and I got three metal plates on the right side of my face. VO: These cargo thieves mean business. SEW: You have your more organised guys that drops off guys that, offload the trucks and then come fetch the stuff as in a bakkie or a taxi VO: Something the recovery drivers have witnessed. DRIVER 2: There was a super link loaded with plank, there was security guards there everything – so when I pick the truck up – I got it on it’s wheels – the plank – the load fell – the guys that were guarding the load they were pointed with firearms – they want to help themselves to the load – tractors were there, vans were there DEVI: Tractors? DRIVER 2: Tractors! With trailers… they load everything. VO: And with cargo theft not being a priority crime, very few arrests are made. NEIL: There’s times when we opened up cases for stuff stolen but we never really got any feedback from there… I don’t know if the cases are getting investigated. VO: Brigadier Naicker accepts there are challenges with these types of cases. JAY: The investigation becomes a problem because the communities that benefit from it don’t talk. It’s very difficult. SEW: It comes free to the criminal, he can sell it as reduced, almost for nothing and he’s still makes money. Needless to say the end- user is saving // they score as well // purely on the basis of this being a win – win – this aint going away. VO: Spotter Vusi agrees, there’s even a black market for the stolen cargo. SPOTTER: It’s easier to sell it to spaza shop. Lets say for example the 10kg rice is R100 by the store – now we are going to sell it for R50 – just to get the quick bucks. DEVI: how much would you make from load? SPOTTER: usually every week we were making about 6 grand, 6000 or 7000 each week because we were selling the things cheaper VO: Vusi says there is a big demand for stolen goods. SPOTTER: people from the spaza shops were starting to put the order to us - if they want the rice, if they want the sugar they came to us they put the orders – so, we take from the trucks. JAY: And somehow people have the impression that if a truck is involved in an accident they are entitled to the load and that is not the case – there is an owner for those goods, and you can’t just remove it with out permission – it’s still theft. PROMOS PROMO1 VO: Cargo theft is rife in South Africa. SEW: // The criminal or community’s mindset is it’s insured – why worry? VO: If you add up the losses - it’s a massive hit to the economy. PROMO 2 VO: Cargo theft is a growing trend in South Africa– everything is up for the taking - with entire loads disappearing in minutes. GLYNN: We’ve had all sorts stolen – from bags of fertiliser to gas bottles – you name it, it will get stolen. // INT6 M3 PROMO 3 VO: Cargo Theft is more organised than you’d think – brazen gangs target specific trucks to get to the loot. SPOTTER: we go to the trucks and jump to the trucks while it is moving up in the mountain // INT1 M2 VO: We expose this growing trend. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Trucks are looted every single day in South Africa – we expose this growing trend and ask what it costs the economy?
metadata.Summary: 90% of what you buy and consume is transported by road – that’s over R456 billion worth of goods on the road every year – making the transport industry a prime target for opportunistic and organised thieves. We expose this crime trend – looking at the contributing factors and impacts on the economy.
metadata.Further information: When a truck breaks down in certain rural areas – you can be sure that the cargo will be gone in a matter of minutes. In some cases where roads are challenging and trucks moved at reduced speeds – thieves simply get on and loot the moving truck. WHO’S BEHIND IT? It’s both opportunistic and organized. People from surrounding communities will loot when the opportunity arises. While others will specifically target trucks and come prepared with vehicles to move the goods. WHY DOESN’T ANYONE SPEAK OUT? Firstly – stolen goods are FREE – so if you are to sell it even at a reduced price you are still making a profit. Should you buy it at a reduced price – you are still winning because it’s cheaper than market value. So no one wants to snitch on the looting thieves – because everyone except the transporter benefits. IMPACT ON TRANSPORT INDUSTRY The economy looses millions of rands annually to stolen cargo. It cost the transporters increased insurance premiums and pushes up transport costs which eventually translates to increased consumer goods prices. SECONDARY DAMAGE But it goes beyond the loss of the cargo. Often trucks are damaged – tyres slashed, tarps cut – this all costs money and means that the trucks will not be operational for a few days costing even more money in lost revenue. VIOLENCE In many instances the looters have turned violent when transporters and the police have tried to stop them. Some drivers are fearful of driving certain routes with consumer goods. There are cases of drivers being shot at, attacked with broken bottles. There have even been horrific cases where drivers have died in accidents and looters continued stealing the cargo despite the driver’s body lying there. POLICE The police is not effective at all. There are videos where they simply stand by as the looters carry away cargo without intervening. SECURITY This type of cargo theft has opened up a market for armed security escorts. 95% of big transport companies make used of additional security to escort their trucks through certain areas. If they don’t they will get targeted. HOW TO DO IT - FOOTAGE – we have great videos of cargo being stolen from moving trucks and accident scenes. - STING – we have a transporter that has offered us a load to move through an area where we expect stealing to take place. We will wait nearby and intervene – filming everything as it happens. INTERVIEWS - BIG TRANSPORTER – impact from a national perspective, the extent of the looting and threats to drivers. - SMALL TRANSPORTER – often they can’t afford the security and are at a greater risk. - ARMED ESCORTS – they explain the MO and level opportunism vs organized efforts. - POLICE – why aren’t they acting – it’s criminality right in front of them. - INSURANCE – impact on the economy – extent of the losses. - DRIVERS – We hear first hand from drivers that have been attacked and threatened and why they are scared to drive certain routes.
